title: Scylla. Sibylla. Digressus
titleEn: Scylla, the Sibyl's Leaves and the Farewells — Aeneid III.410–505
part: Scylla, the Sibyl's Leaves and the Farewells (III.410–505)
about: Helenus, the seer-king of Buthrotum, goes on with the prophecy he began in the last part. When Aeneas has crossed to Sicily he is to keep to the left-hand shore and take the long way round, for the narrow strait was once torn from Italy by force and is now guarded on the right by Scylla, a maiden above and a sea-monster below, and on the left by Charybdis, who gulps the sea down three times and throws it back at the stars. Better to round the far cape and lose time than to see Scylla once. Then the one thing Helenus will say again and again: Aeneas must first of all win over Juno with prayers, vows and gifts. At Cumae he will find the frenzied Sibyl, who writes her oracles on leaves and arranges them in her cave, but lets a draught from the door scatter them and never troubles to put them back, so that visitors leave without an answer and hate the place. Aeneas must not let his crew's impatience or a fair wind keep him from asking her himself; she will tell him of Italy's peoples and the wars to come and how to bear each trial. The seer ends with the blessing “Go on your way, and let your deeds bear mighty Troy up to the skies.” Gifts follow: gold, carved ivory, silver, bronze cauldrons from Dodona, and the corselet and helmet of Neoptolemus, with horses, guides, extra oarsmen and arms for the crew. Anchises has the fleet made ready, and Helenus greets him politely, tells him the land of Ausonia lies before him but he must sail past this nearest part of it, and then breaks off to stop delaying the rising wind. Andromache, sad at the last parting, brings Ascanius embroidered garments and a Phrygian cloak, and says that he is all that is left her of her own Astyanax. Aeneas answers through his tears: they are at rest, but he is called from one fate to the next; if he ever reaches the Tiber he and they will make the two Troys, in Epirus and in Hesperia, one in spirit, and let that charge pass to their descendants.

sentences.t:
Ast ubi digressum Siculae te admoverit orae
ventus, et angusti rarescent claustra Pelori,
laeva tibi tellus et longo laeva petantur
aequora circuitu:
sentences.l:
But when, departed, to the Sicilian shore you the wind shall have brought near,
and of narrow Pelorus the barriers shall grow thin,
the left land for you and the left
waters be sought by a long circuit:
sentences.i: But when, having left, the wind shall have brought you to the Sicilian shore, and the bars of narrow Pelorus begin to open, let the left-hand land and the left-hand water be your goal, by a long detour:
sentences.n: The prophecy of Helenus, begun in the last part, goes on in a new paragraph. 'Ast' is an old form of 'at', 'but'. 'ubi… admoverit… rarescent' — 'ubi' ('when') with a future perfect, 'shall have moved you to', and a future, 'shall grow thin': the clause looks ahead to the day Aeneas arrives. 'digressum' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'digredior', 'departed', agreeing with 'te'. 'Siculae orae' is a dative of the place to which. 'angusti… Pelori' — Pelorus is the north-eastern cape of Sicily, and the 'claustra' ('bars, barriers') are the narrow headlands that seem to close the strait until you get close, when they open out. 'laeva… tellus et… laeva… aequora' — the repeated 'laeva' ('left') stresses which side to take; 'petantur' is a present subjunctive used as a command (jussive), passive, with the plural subjects 'tellus' and 'aequora', and 'tibi' is the person who must do it. 'longo… circuitu' (ablative of means) — the long way round Sicily. The colon prepares the other half of the instruction.

sentences.t: dextrum fuge litus et undas.
sentences.l: the right shore flee, and the waves.
sentences.i: keep far from the right-hand shore and its waters.
sentences.n: 'fuge' is the imperative of 'fugio', 'flee, shun'. 'dextrum… litus et undas' — 'dextrum' is neuter, agreeing with 'litus' ('shore'), and 'undas' ('waves') is its partner: avoid the right-hand coast and its water. In the next lines we learn why: Scylla holds the right-hand side.

sentences.t:
Haec loca vi quondam et vasta convolsa ruina—
tantum aevi longinqua valet mutare vetustas—
dissiluisse ferunt, cum protinus utraque tellus
una foret;
sentences.l:
These places by force once and by a vast collapse torn up—
so much of age far-off antiquity has power to change—
to have split apart, they say, when continuously each land
was one;
sentences.i: These lands, they say, once split apart, wrenched by violence and a mighty upheaval — so much can the long reach of far-off time change — when each shore was joined to the other in one unbroken stretch;
sentences.n: 'ferunt' ('they say') takes an accusative and infinitive: 'haec loca… dissiluisse', 'these places… split apart' (the perfect infinitive of 'dissilio', 'leap apart'). The old belief, which Virgil adopts, was that Sicily had been torn from Italy by an earthquake. 'convolsa' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'convulsa') is a perfect passive participle, neuter plural, agreeing with 'loca': 'torn up'. 'vi… et vasta… ruina' — two ablatives of means, 'by force and by a vast collapse'. The dashes enclose a remark thrown in by the speaker: 'tantum aevi… mutare' is 'so much of age… to change': 'tantum' is taken as the object of 'mutare' with 'aevi' depending on it, though the exact construction is not certain; 'valet' with an infinitive meaning 'has the power to'; 'longinqua vetustas' ('far-distant antiquity') is the subject. 'cum… utraque tellus una foret' — 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive 'foret' (an older form of 'esset': 'fore' forms come up constantly in verse), 'when each land was one'; 'protinus' here means 'continuously, in one unbroken line'. The semicolon ends the clause, and the sea's action follows.

sentences.t:
venit medio vi pontus et undis
Hesperium Siculo latus abscidit, arvaque et urbes
litore diductas angusto interluit aestu.
sentences.l:
came in the middle by force the sea, and with waves
the Hesperian side from the Sicilian cut off, and fields and cities
by a shore drawn apart with a narrow tide flows between.
sentences.i: the sea came through the midst with force and with its waves, and cut the western side from the Sicilian, and now runs between fields and cities that a shore keeps apart, in a narrow tide.
sentences.n: 'venit… pontus' — 'pontus' ('the sea') is the subject; 'medio' ('in the middle') is used almost as an adverb, and its exact construction is not certain, but the sense is not in doubt. 'vi et undis' are ablatives of means. 'Hesperium Siculo latus abscidit' — 'Hesperium' ('western', i.e. Italian) agrees with 'latus' ('side'), and 'Siculo', dative, goes with the compound verb 'abscidit' ('cut off from'), with 'lateri' understood. 'arvaque et urbes litore diductas' — 'diductas' is a perfect passive participle, 'drawn apart', agreeing with 'arva' and 'urbes'; 'litore' (ablative of means) is the strait's own coast. 'interluit' is 'flows between', present: the strait is still there. 'angusto… aestu' is an ablative of manner; 'aestus' is 'tide, surge'. The dividing of the two coasts is explained for the sake of the next lines.

sentences.t:
Dextrum Scylla latus, laevum implacata Charybdis
obsidet, atque imo barathri ter gurgite vastos
sorbet in abruptum fluctus, rursusque sub auras
erigit alternos et sidera verberat unda.
sentences.l:
The right side Scylla, the left unappeased Charybdis
besets, and in the lowest of the chasm, thrice, in the whirlpool, the vast
sucks into the sheer drop the waves, and again up under the breezes
raises in turn, and the stars lashes with the wave.
sentences.i: Scylla holds the right-hand side and unappeased Charybdis the left; from the depth of her chasm, three times over, Charybdis gulps vast waves down into the sheer pit, and again lifts them up in turn into the air and lashes the stars with the surge.
sentences.n: 'obsidet' is singular though it has two subjects, 'Scylla' and 'Charybdis'; it is shared out between them by the parallel 'dextrum… latus, laevum': one watches each side. 'implacata' is an adjective from 'placo' with the negative 'in-', 'unappeased, implacable', agreeing with 'Charybdis'. 'imo barathri… gurgite' — 'barathri' is the genitive of the Greek loan 'barathrum', 'chasm', and 'imo gurgite' ('in the lowest whirlpool') is an ablative of place; 'ter' ('three times') goes with 'sorbet', and 'vastos' ('vast') agrees with 'fluctus' on the next line. The detail that Charybdis swallows the sea three times comes from the Odyssey (Book 12), the model for this whole passage. 'sorbet in abruptum' — 'abruptum' is a neuter adjective used as a noun, 'the steep place, the sheer drop'. 'rursusque sub auras erigit alternos' — 'sub' with the accusative of motion, 'up toward'; 'alternos' (accusative plural, masculine) is used in place of an adverb, 'in turn', and 'fluctus' is understood from the line before. 'sidera verberat unda' — 'unda' is an ablative of means, singular for plural.

sentences.t:
At Scyllam caecis cohibet spelunca latebris,
ora exsertantem et navis in saxa trahentem.
sentences.l:
But Scylla in blind hiding-places a cave encloses,
her faces thrusting out and ships onto the rocks dragging.
sentences.i: But Scylla a cave holds shut in its dark recesses, though she keeps thrusting out her faces and dragging ships onto the rocks.
sentences.n: 'At' is a contrast: Charybdis is in the open water, but Scylla is hidden. 'caecis… latebris' is an ablative of place; 'caecus' ('blind') here means 'dark, hidden', and 'latebrae' are 'hiding-places'. 'cohibet' is 'holds in, confines'. 'ora exsertantem et navis in saxa trahentem' — two present participles (accusative singular, agreeing with 'Scyllam'): 'exsertantem' is from 'exserto', 'keep thrusting out' (a frequentative of 'exsero'), with 'ora' ('mouths, faces') as object; 'navis' is the accusative plural in -is (you'll see this constantly). In the Odyssey (12) Scylla has six heads that snatch men from passing ships; Virgil gives only the gesture.

sentences.t:
Prima hominis facies et pulchro pectore virgo
pube tenus, postrema immani corpore pristis,
delphinum caudas utero commissa luporum.
sentences.l:
First the face of a man and with lovely breast a maiden
to the groin, last, of immense body, a sea monster,
of dolphins the tails to the belly of wolves joined.
sentences.i: Above, a human face and a maiden's lovely breast down to the groin; below, a sea-monster of enormous body, with dolphins' tails grafted onto a belly of wolves.
sentences.n: A nominal sentence: no verb is expressed ('est' is understood). 'Prima… facies' ('the first part is a human face') and 'postrema… pristis' ('the last part is a sea-monster') stand against each other; 'virgo' is a second nominative in the first half. 'pulchro pectore' and 'immani corpore' are ablatives of description. 'pube tenus' — 'tenus' ('as far as') follows its noun, and its noun is in the ablative. 'pristis' (Greenough's form; the Latin Library prints 'pistrix') is a sea-monster, a shark or whale. 'delphinum' is the old genitive plural (-um for -orum, as 'divom' and 'virum', you'll see this constantly), 'of dolphins'. 'commissa' is a perfect passive participle, feminine, 'joined together', agreeing with the monster as a whole: 'caudas' ('tails') are what is joined to the 'utero luporum' ('belly of wolves', a form which is dative or ablative); the grammar is loose, but the picture is clear. The account is of a monster seen from above and below.

sentences.t:
Praestat Trinacrii metas lustrare Pachyni
cessantem, longos et circumflectere cursus,
quam semel informem vasto vidisse sub antro
Scyllam, et caeruleis canibus resonantia saxa.
sentences.l:
It is better of Trinacrian Pachynus the turning posts to round,
lingering, and long courses to bend around,
than once misshapen under the vast cave to have seen
Scylla, and the rocks echoing with sea-dark dogs.
sentences.i: Better to go round the turning-post of Sicilian Pachynus, and lose time over it, and bend your course in a long detour, than once to look on misshapen Scylla under her vast cave, and the rocks that echo with her dark-blue hounds.
sentences.n: 'Praestat' is impersonal ('it is better') and takes infinitives as its subject: 'lustrare… et circumflectere', 'to go round… and to bend round'; 'quam… vidisse', 'than to have seen' (a perfect infinitive). 'Trinacrii… Pachyni' — Pachynus is the south-eastern cape of Sicily, and 'metas' (accusative plural, 'turning-posts') is the language of a chariot race, where the 'meta' is the post to be rounded. 'cessantem' is a present participle, accusative, agreeing with the subject of the infinitives ('you', not expressed): 'lingering, taking your time'. 'longos et circumflectere cursus' — 'et' here joins the two infinitives, though it follows the first word of the second. 'semel' (once) is the point: a single sight is worse than the whole delay. 'informem… Scyllam' — 'informis' is 'shapeless, misshapen'. 'caeruleis canibus resonantia saxa' — 'resonantia' is a present participle (neuter plural) agreeing with 'saxa', and 'canibus' is an ablative of cause, 'echoing with dogs'; 'caeruleus' is 'dark blue', the colour of the sea.

sentences.t:
Praeterea, si qua est Heleno prudentia, vati
si qua fides, animum si veris implet Apollo,
unum illud tibi, nate dea, proque omnibus unum
praedicam, et repetens iterumque iterumque monebo:
sentences.l:
Besides, if any is for Helenus foresight, for the seer
if any trust, if the mind with truths Apollo fills,
one thing that, to you, son of a goddess, and for all things one
I shall foretell, and repeating again and again shall warn:
sentences.i: Furthermore, if Helenus has any foresight, if the seer is owed any trust, if Apollo fills his mind with truth, there is one thing, goddess-born, one thing in place of all the rest, that I shall tell you in advance, and, saying it again and again, shall urge upon you:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'si qua est Heleno prudentia' — 'est' with a dative is the dative of possession (you'll see this constantly): 'if there is to Helenus any foresight'; 'qua' is the indefinite after 'si', agreeing with 'prudentia'. Helenus speaks of himself by name, a formal tone suited to a prophet. 'vati si qua fides' — 'vati', the seer, is in apposition to 'Heleno', and 'est' is understood. 'si… si… si' is a triple condition, 'if… if… if', whose conclusion is the main clause 'praedicam… monebo'. 'animum si veris implet Apollo' — 'implet' takes the ablative: 'fills the mind with true things'; 'veris' is a neuter plural used as a noun. 'unum illud… unum' is repeated at the beginning and end of the phrase for emphasis; 'pro omnibus' means 'in place of everything', the one thing that matters more than the rest. 'nate dea' — 'nate' is the vocative of 'natus', 'dea' an ablative of origin: 'son born of a goddess' (as in lines 311 and 374). 'praedicam… monebo' — two futures; 'repetens' is a present participle, 'repeating', and 'iterumque iterumque' ('again and again') makes the urgency plain. The colon introduces the instruction itself.

sentences.t: Iunonis magnae primum prece numen adora;
sentences.l: Of Juno great first with prayer the godhead adore;
sentences.i: First of all, with prayer, do honour to the divine power of great Juno;
sentences.n: 'adora' is the imperative of 'adoro', 'to worship, to address in prayer'. 'Iunonis magnae… numen' — the genitive and its noun are split by 'primum prece' (hyperbaton), so the words 'Juno' and 'great' come first, set before the verb. 'numen' is the divine power or will of a god. 'prece' is an ablative of means. Juno is the goddess who has persecuted the Trojans since Book I, and Helenus makes her the first concern; Virgil has mentioned that Fate and Juno do not allow Helenus to tell everything (3.379–380).

sentences.t:
Iunoni cane vota libens, dominamque potentem
supplicibus supera donis:
sentences.l:
To Juno chant vows willingly, and the mistress powerful
with suppliant gifts overcome:
sentences.i: Chant your vows to Juno with a willing heart, and win the powerful lady over with the gifts of a suppliant:
sentences.n: 'Iunoni' is a dative of the indirect object, the goddess to whom the vows are chanted. 'cane vota' — 'cano' is 'sing, chant', here 'recite' a vow in the proper words. 'libens' is a nominative adjective, 'willingly, gladly', a word in the language of religion that tells the gods the offering is freely given. 'dominamque potentem' — 'domina' is 'mistress, lady', a title of respect for a goddess. 'supera' is the imperative of 'supero', 'overcome'; 'supplicibus donis' is an ablative of means, 'with suppliant gifts' (the gifts of one who kneels). The colon introduces what follows from doing this.

sentences.t:
sic denique victor
Trinacria finis Italos mittere relicta.
sentences.l:
thus at last, a victor,
to Italian borders to send yourself, Trinacria left behind.
sentences.i: so, in the end, you will make your way to the bounds of Italy as a victor, with Sicily left behind.
sentences.n: 'sic denique' — 'thus at last'. 'victor' is a nominative predicate, 'as a victor'. 'mittere' is an infinitive where the sentence seems to want a verb: it stands for 'you will send yourself, you will go', and commentators do not agree on its exact construction, though the meaning is not in doubt. 'finis Italos' — 'finis' is the accusative plural of 'finis' in -is (you'll see this constantly), 'Italian borders'. 'Trinacria relicta' is an ablative absolute: 'Sicily having been left'; 'Trinacria' is the island's Greek name, 'the three-cornered'.

sentences.t:
Huc ubi delatus Cumaeam accesseris urbem,
divinosque lacus, et Averna sonantia silvis,
insanam vatem aspicies, quae rupe sub ima
fata canit, foliisque notas et nomina mandat.
sentences.l:
Hither when carried you shall have approached the Cumaean city,
and the divine lakes, and Avernus sounding with woods,
a frenzied seer you will behold, who beneath the lowest rock
fates sings, and to leaves marks and names entrusts.
sentences.i: When you have been carried here and have come to the city of Cumae, the sacred lakes, and Avernus murmuring with its forests, you will see a frenzied prophetess who, beneath the deepest rock, sings the fates and entrusts signs and names to leaves.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Helenus turns from the sea to the land. 'Huc ubi delatus… accesseris' — 'ubi' with the future perfect 'accesseris' ('when you shall have approached'), and 'delatus' a perfect passive participle, 'carried down' (to the coast), agreeing with 'you'. 'accesseris' takes an accusative ('Cumaeam urbem'), as do 'divinosque lacus' and 'Averna sonantia silvis': all three are objects of the one verb. 'Averna' is a neuter plural, the district and lake of Avernus, and 'sonantia' ('sounding') is a present participle, with 'silvis' an ablative of cause or means. 'insanam vatem aspicies' is the main clause: 'insana' means 'frenzied, possessed', the state of a prophetess when the god is in her. 'quae rupe sub ima fata canit' — 'sub' stands in the middle of its phrase, between the noun and its adjective, 'beneath the lowest rock'; 'canit' is 'sings, proclaims in verse'. 'foliisque notas et nomina mandat' — 'mandat' is 'entrusts', with a dative ('to leaves') and two objects, 'notas' (marks, signs, as letters) and 'nomina' (names, the words themselves). The Sibyl of Cumae is the prophetess whom Aeneas will meet in Book VI.

sentences.t:
Quaecumque in foliis descripsit carmina virgo,
digerit in numerum, atque antro seclusa relinquit.
sentences.l:
Whatever on leaves has written verses the maiden,
she arranges into order, and in the cave shut away leaves them.
sentences.i: Whatever oracles the maiden has written down on leaves she sets in order, and leaves them shut away in her cave.
sentences.n: 'Quaecumque… carmina' — the relative clause comes first and contains its own antecedent, 'carmina': 'whatever songs'; in the main clause 'ea' ('them') is understood as the object of both 'digerit' and 'relinquit'. 'carmina' here are the verses or oracles, 'songs' because they are in verse. 'descripsit' is a perfect: 'has written out'. 'digerit in numerum' — 'digero' is 'arrange, set in order'; 'in numerum' is 'into a series'. 'seclusa' is a perfect passive participle (neuter plural) agreeing with the understood object, 'shut away'; 'antro' is an ablative of place. The Sibyl is called 'virgo', 'maiden', as a prophetess of Apollo.

sentences.t: Illa manent immota locis, neque ab ordine cedunt;
sentences.l: Those remain unmoved in their places, nor from the order depart;
sentences.i: There they stay, unmoved in their places, and keep their order;
sentences.n: 'Illa' ('those', the verses) is the subject. 'immota' is a neuter plural predicate, 'unmoved'. 'locis' is an ablative of place with no preposition, 'in their places' (a poetic use). 'neque ab ordine cedunt' — 'cedo' with 'ab' is 'to depart from'. So long as nothing disturbs them, nothing changes; the next lines say what happens when something does.

sentences.t:
verum eadem, verso tenuis cum cardine ventus
impulit et teneras turbavit ianua frondes,
numquam deinde cavo volitantia prendere saxo,
nec revocare situs aut iungere carmina curat:
sentences.l:
but these same, when, the hinge turned, a thin wind
has driven, and the tender leaves has stirred the door,
never after, flying about in the hollow rock, to catch,
nor to call back their places or join the verses she cares:
sentences.i: But those same verses, when the hinge has turned and a thin wind has blown in and the door has stirred the delicate foliage, she never afterwards cares to catch as they flutter in the hollow rock, nor to call them back to their places or to join the oracles together:
sentences.n: 'verum eadem' — 'verum' is 'but', and 'eadem' is neuter plural, 'the same ones', that is the verses (the 'carmina' of the last unit), and is the object of 'prendere' below; the leaves are 'frondes', which is feminine. 'verso tenuis cum cardine ventus impulit et teneras turbavit ianua frondes' — 'cum' with a perfect indicative means 'whenever' (a repeated event). 'verso… cardine' is an ablative absolute ('the hinge having turned'), and 'tenuis' goes with 'ventus', 'a thin, slight wind'. 'impulit' and 'turbavit' are two perfects, and the word 'ianua' (the door) is read in different ways: as the subject of 'turbavit' (the door stirs the leaves as it swings) or as an ablative (the wind comes through the door). Either way the sense is that a draught from the opening door scatters the leaves. 'numquam deinde' — 'never after that'. 'cavo volitantia prendere saxo' — 'volitantia' is a present participle (neuter plural) agreeing with the understood 'ea' ('them'), 'fluttering', from 'volito', 'flit about'; 'cavo… saxo' is an ablative of place. 'nec revocare situs aut iungere carmina curat' — the subject of 'curat' is the Sibyl, and 'curo' takes a present infinitive ('cares to'); 'situs' is the accusative plural of 'situs' (fourth declension), 'positions'. 'numquam… nec… aut' — the negatives pile up for emphasis, as is normal in Latin. The colon prepares the result.

sentences.t: inconsulti abeunt, sedemque odere Sibyllae.
sentences.l: unadvised they depart, and the seat of the Sibyl have come to hate.
sentences.i: and the visitors go away with no answer, and loathe the Sibyl's dwelling.
sentences.n: The subject changes: 'inconsulti' is a nominative plural, 'unadvised, without having had advice', and the people who have consulted her are meant. 'abeunt' is 'go away'. 'odere' is 'oderunt' (the ending -ere for -erunt: you'll see this constantly), the perfect of 'odi', 'I hate', which is a perfect in form and a present in meaning; so 'they hate'. 'sedem Sibyllae' is the cave. The picture is of petitioners who find the leaves in confusion.

sentences.t: Hic tibi ne qua morae fuerint dispendia tanti,—
sentences.l: Here to you lest any of delay losses be of so great a worth,—
sentences.i: Here, let no loss from delay count for so much with you —
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Hic' is the adverb, 'here' (at Cumae). 'ne qua… fuerint dispendia' — 'ne' with a perfect subjunctive is a prohibition ('let there not have been'); 'qua' here is the neuter plural form of the indefinite after 'ne' ('any'), agreeing with 'dispendia' ('losses, wasted costs'). 'morae' is a genitive, 'of delay'. 'tanti' is a genitive of value, 'of so much worth': let no cost of delay seem to you so great. The dash begins a parenthesis, which ends at 455 with another dash, and the sentence is resumed with 'quin adeas'.

sentences.t:
quamvis increpitent socii, et vi cursus in altum
vela vocet, possisque sinus implere secundos,—
sentences.l:
although chide your comrades, and with force the voyage to the deep
the sails call, and you be able to fill the favouring folds,—
sentences.i: however loudly your companions protest, however the voyage summons your sails out to the deep, and however well you could fill your canvas with a fair wind —
sentences.n: 'quamvis' with a present subjunctive is 'however much', concessive: 'increpitent', 'vocet', 'possis' are all in that mood. 'increpitent' is a frequentative of 'increpo', 'keep on shouting at, scolding'. 'et vi cursus in altum vela vocet' — 'cursus' (nominative singular) is the voyage, the subject of 'vocet', 'calls' the sails, with 'vi' ('with force') an ablative of manner; 'in altum' is 'to the deep sea'. 'possisque sinus implere secundos' — 'possis' is the subjunctive, 'you be able', 'sinus' (accusative plural) are the swelling folds of the sails, and 'secundos' is 'favouring' (the wind). The dash closes the parenthesis begun at 453.

sentences.t:
quin adeas vatem precibusque oracula poscas
ipsa canat, vocemque volens atque ora resolvat.
sentences.l:
that you go to the seer, and with prayers the oracles ask
that she herself sing, and, willing, her voice and lips set free.
sentences.i: to stop you from going to the prophetess and begging her with prayers to sing her oracles herself and, of her own will, to loose her voice and her lips.
sentences.n: 'quin adeas' — 'quin' with the subjunctive follows a negative of hindering or delay, 'that you do not go', 'but that you go': the whole sentence means 'let no delay stop you from going'. 'poscas' is a second subjunctive on the same footing. 'vatem' is the object of 'adeas'; 'precibus' is an ablative of means. 'oracula poscas ipsa canat' — the request ('poscas') is followed by a bare subjunctive 'canat', 'that she herself sing', with 'ut' left out; 'ipsa' ('she herself') refers to the Sibyl, as against her leaves. 'vocemque volens atque ora resolvat' — 'volens' is a nominative adjective, 'willing', and 'resolvo' is 'loosen, set free', with 'vocem' and 'ora' as objects. The Sibyl has to give her answer by speaking; the scattered leaves cannot be trusted.

sentences.t:
Illa tibi Italiae populos venturaque bella,
et quo quemque modo fugiasque ferasque laborem
expediet, cursusque dabit venerata secundos.
sentences.l:
She to you of Italy the peoples and the wars to come,
and in what way each you may both flee and bear trial
will unfold, and courses will give, having been worshipped, favourable.
sentences.i: She will set out for you the peoples of Italy and the wars to come, and how you may avoid or endure each hardship, and, if you honour her, will grant you a prosperous course.
sentences.n: 'Illa' is the Sibyl. 'expediet' (a future, in line 460) governs three objects: 'populos', 'bella' (with 'venturaque', a future participle, 'about to come') and an indirect question. 'et quo quemque modo fugiasque ferasque laborem' — 'quo modo' ('in what way') begins the indirect question, whose verbs 'fugias' and 'feras' are present subjunctives; 'quemque… laborem' ('each trial') is the object of both, split by the verbs. 'cursusque dabit venerata secundos' — 'venerata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'veneror', here with a passive sense ('having been worshipped'), and carries a condition: if she is honoured. 'cursus… secundos' are favourable courses, i.e. a prosperous voyage.

sentences.t: Haec sunt, quae nostra liceat te voce moneri.
sentences.l: These are the things that by our voice it may be allowed you to be warned.
sentences.i: That is all I am permitted to tell you.
sentences.n: 'Haec sunt, quae… liceat' — the relative clause has a subjunctive, 'liceat', because it says what sort of things these are (a clause of characteristic): 'the things which it may be permitted'. 'liceat te voce moneri' — 'liceo' is an impersonal verb here, with an accusative and infinitive: 'it is allowed (for) you to be warned'. 'nostra voce' is an ablative of means, 'nostra' being the plural for the singular, a poetic habit; the speaker is Helenus. The line closes what Helenus has said he can tell: the Fates and Juno forbid more (3.379–380).

sentences.t: Vade age, et ingentem factis fer ad aethera Troiam.”
sentences.l: Go, come now, and mighty by deeds carry to the heavens Troy.”
sentences.i: Go on your way, and let your deeds bear mighty Troy up to the skies.”
sentences.n: 'Vade age' — 'vade' is the imperative of 'vado', 'go', and 'age' is 'come on, now' (the same 'age' as in 'fare age', 364). 'et ingentem factis fer ad aethera Troiam' — 'fer' is the imperative of 'fero', 'carry'; 'ingentem' is an ordinary adjective with 'Troiam' ('mighty Troy'), set early in the line, apart from its noun at the end; 'factis' is an ablative of means, 'by deeds'; 'aethera' is a Greek accusative singular, 'the upper air, the sky'. The closing mark ” in Greenough's print stands after the full stop, and ends the speech that Helenus began at 374, in the last part. Troy's greatness will be in the new city, not the old.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam vates sic ore effatus amico est,
dona dehinc auro gravia sectoque elephanto
imperat ad navis ferri,
sentences.l:
Which things after the seer thus with friendly mouth has spoken,
gifts then with gold heavy and with cut ivory
he orders to the ships to be carried,
sentences.i: When the seer had spoken thus with kindly lips, he orders gifts heavy with gold and cut ivory to be carried to the ships,
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Aeneas's narration resumes. 'Quae postquam… effatus est' — 'quae' is a connecting relative (you'll see this constantly), the neuter plural object of 'effatus est': 'after he had said these things'; 'postquam' with a perfect indicative is 'after'; 'effatus est' is the perfect of the deponent 'effor', 'speak out'. 'ore… amico' is an ablative of manner. 'dona dehinc auro gravia sectoque elephanto' — 'gravia' ('heavy') agrees with 'dona'; 'auro' and 'sectoque elephanto' are ablatives (of respect, 'heavy with') ; 'elephanto' is used for ivory, and 'sectoque' ('cut, sawn', the Latin Library prints 'ac secto') means ivory cut in plates. 'imperat… ferri' — 'impero' here takes an accusative and passive infinitive: 'dona… ferri', 'orders gifts to be carried'; 'ad navis' has the accusative plural in -is. The comma is where the long list of gifts is split.

sentences.t:
stipatque carinis
ingens argentum, Dodonaeosque lebetas,
loricam consertam hamis auroque trilicem,
et conum insignis galeae cristasque comantis,
arma Neoptolemi;
sentences.l:
and stows in the keels
great silver, and Dodonaean cauldrons,
a corselet linked with rings and with gold three-ply,
and the cone of a distinguished helmet and the crests plumed,
the arms of Neoptolemus;
sentences.i: and stows in the hulls a great weight of silver, and cauldrons from Dodona, a corselet of linked mail, three-ply with gold, and the cone of a splendid helmet with its flowing crests — the arms of Neoptolemus;
sentences.n: 'stipat… carinis ingens argentum' — 'stipo' is 'pack, cram'; 'argentum' is the object and 'carinis' ('keels') stands for 'ships' by synecdoche (a part for the whole), in the dative or ablative of place. 'Dodonaeosque lebetas' — Dodona, in Epirus, is the oracle of Zeus, so 'Dodonaeos' means 'of Dodona'; 'lebetas' is a Greek accusative plural, 'cauldrons'. 'loricam consertam hamis auroque trilicem' — 'consertam' is a perfect passive participle, 'linked together', with 'hamis' ('with rings, hooks') as an ablative of means; 'trilicem' (accusative, agreeing with 'loricam') is 'three-ply, of triple thread', with 'auro' as its ablative. 'conum insignis galeae cristasque comantis' — 'conus' is the cone or peak on a helmet that holds the plume; 'insignis' is here a genitive singular (-is) agreeing with 'galeae'; 'cristas… comantis' is an accusative plural in -is, from 'comans', 'hairy, crested'. 'arma Neoptolemi' sums up the last three items (corselet, cone, crests) as an apposition. Neoptolemus, also called Pyrrhus, is the son of Achilles who killed Priam (Book II) and took Andromache; his arms are now given to the Trojans.

sentences.t: sunt et sua dona parenti.
sentences.l: There are also his own gifts for my father.
sentences.i: My father, too, has gifts of his own;
sentences.n: 'sunt… dona… parenti' — 'parenti', a dative with 'sunt', is the dative of possession (you'll see this constantly): 'there are gifts to my parent'; Aeneas means Anchises. 'sua' ('his own') points back to the dative, the person who receives them. 'et' means 'also'. The gifts for Anchises are listed apart from the gifts just named.

sentences.t: Addit equos, additque duces;
sentences.l: He adds horses, and adds guides;
sentences.i: He adds horses, and adds guides;
sentences.n: A half-line: Virgil left some verses unfinished (these 'hemistichs' number about fifty-eight in the whole poem), and Greenough prints this one short, as 'Addit equos, additque duces;' with the rest of the six feet missing. 'Addit… additque' repeats the verb with 'que' on the second, 'he adds… and adds'. 'duces' here means guides or pilots, men to show the way, not generals. The semicolon runs on to the next verse, which lists more of the help.

sentences.t: remigium supplet;
sentences.l: oarage he makes up;
sentences.i: he makes up the oarsmen;
sentences.n: 'remigium' is a collective noun: 'the rowing, the body of oarsmen' (the crews). 'supplet' is 'fills up, makes good' what is missing, here the crews' numbers.

sentences.t: socios simul instruit armis.
sentences.l: his comrades at the same time he equips with arms.
sentences.i: and at the same time arms the companions.
sentences.n: 'socios' is the object of 'instruit', 'equips, supplies'; 'armis' is an ablative of means, 'with arms'; 'simul' ('at the same time') is an adverb. The 'socios' are Aeneas's men.

sentences.t:
Interea classem velis aptare iubebat
Anchises, fieret vento mora ne qua ferenti.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile the fleet with sails to fit out was ordering
Anchises, so that there be not for the wind carrying any delay.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Anchises was ordering the fleet to be fitted out with sails, so that no delay should hold up the fair wind that was bearing them.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'iubebat aptare' — 'iubeo' with an infinitive and no subject expressed ('he ordered [them] to fit out'); 'classem' is the object of 'aptare', and 'velis' an ablative of means. The imperfect 'iubebat' sets the scene. 'fieret vento mora ne qua ferenti' — 'ne qua mora' is a negative purpose clause with 'fieret' in the imperfect subjunctive ('so that no delay should arise'), after a past main verb; 'qua' agrees with 'mora'; 'vento… ferenti' is a dative, 'for the wind that carries' (a participle, 'fair, bearing them on').

sentences.t: Quem Phoebi interpres multo compellat honore:
sentences.l: Whom Phoebus' interpreter addresses with much honour:
sentences.i: Him the spokesman of Phoebus accosts with great respect:
sentences.n: 'Quem' is a connecting relative, 'him' (Anchises). 'Phoebi interpres' is Helenus, the interpreter of Apollo, as Aeneas called him in 359. 'multo… honore' is an ablative of manner, 'with much honour'. 'compellat' is present tense (the historic present of vivid narrative). The colon introduces what Helenus says.

sentences.i: “Anchises, found worthy of Venus's glorious marriage, the gods' own care, twice snatched from the ruins of Troy, look, the land of Ausonia lies before you;
sentences.n: The opening mark “ begins Helenus's speech to Anchises (475–481). 'Anchise' is the vocative, a Greek form (the Latin Library prints 'Anchisa'); 'dignate' is a vocative, from the perfect participle of the deponent 'dignor', which has a passive sense ('deemed worthy'); 'coniugio… superbo' is an ablative with it, 'of a proud (glorious) union' — Anchises was loved by Venus, the mother of Aeneas. 'cura deum' — 'deum' is the old genitive plural (-um for -orum, you'll see this constantly), 'the gods' care'. 'bis… erepte' — 'erepte' is the vocative of the perfect passive participle, 'snatched out'; 'Pergameis… ruinis' is an ablative of separation, 'from the ruins of Pergamum', that is, Troy. 'bis' ('twice') is explained in different ways, and Virgil does not say which. 'ecce tibi' — 'tibi' is a dative of the person for whom the thing is shown, 'look, for you'. 'Ausonia' is a poetic name for Italy.

sentences.t: hanc arripe velis.
sentences.l: this seize with sails.
sentences.i: make for it with every sail.
sentences.n: 'hanc' is the object, 'this (land)'. 'arripe' is the imperative of 'arripio', 'seize, snatch at', here 'make for it eagerly'. 'velis' is an ablative of means, 'with sails'. The command is the opening of Helenus's advice to the old man, to be balanced by the 'Et tamen' that follows.

sentences.t: Et tamen hanc pelago praeterlabare necesse est;
sentences.l: And yet this by sea you must glide past;
sentences.i: And yet you must slip past this part by sea;
sentences.n: 'Et tamen' is 'and yet', which turns the command around. 'hanc pelago praeterlabare necesse est' — 'praeterlabare' is a present subjunctive (second person singular of the deponent 'praeterlabor', 'glide past'), standing after 'necesse est' without 'ut': 'it is necessary (that) you glide past'; 'hanc' is its object, 'this' nearest coast; 'pelago' is an ablative of means or route, 'by sea', with a poetic word for 'sea'. Helenus has already said (396–402) that the nearest coast of Italy is full of Greek towns, and Aeneas must go round.

sentences.t: Ausoniae pars illa procul, quam pandit Apollo.
sentences.l: of Ausonia that part is far off, which opens Apollo.
sentences.i: that part of Ausonia lies far off, which Apollo lays open to you.
sentences.n: A nominal sentence, 'est' being understood: 'pars illa' is 'that part'. 'Ausoniae' is a genitive of the whole. 'quam pandit Apollo' — 'pandit' is 'opens out, makes known' (the god shows the way), and 'quam' is its object. The archived text has no closing mark after this line, though Helenus has been speaking since 475; the next unit has a second opening mark before 'Vade'. It is one speech of Helenus, with 'ait' set inside it, so the reading text leaves this quotation open and closes it after 'Vade,' in the next unit. The Latin text stays as printed.

sentences.t: “Vade ait O felix nati pietate.
sentences.l: Go,” says he, “O fortunate in the son's devotion.
sentences.i: Go,” he says, “O happy in your son's loyalty.
sentences.n: The archived text has “ before 'Vade' and no closing mark at the end of 479, though Helenus has been speaking since 475 and the same speech runs on to 481. 'ait' is a speech tag, 'he says', set into Helenus's words, so in the English layers the first quotation closes after 'Go,' and a second opens at 'O'; the Latin text stays as printed. 'Vade' is the imperative of 'vado', 'go'. 'ait' is the defective verb 'aio', 'he says'. 'O felix nati pietate' — 'felix' is a vocative (to Anchises), and 'nati pietate' is an ablative of cause or respect, 'in your son's pietas': 'pietas' is dutiful loyalty, Aeneas's defining virtue, whose proof is that he carried Anchises out of Troy.

sentences.t:
Quid ultra
provehor, et fando surgentis demoror austros?”
sentences.l:
Why further
am I carried on, and by speaking the rising south winds do I delay?”
sentences.i: Why do I run on further, and keep holding back the rising winds with my talking?”
sentences.n: 'Quid' is an accusative used as an adverb, 'why?'. 'ultra provehor' — 'provehor' is the passive of 'proveho', 'am I carried forward', in the sense 'do I go on'. 'fando' is the ablative of the gerund of 'for, fari', 'by speaking', an ablative of means. 'surgentis… austros' — 'surgentis' (accusative plural, -is) is a present participle, 'rising'; 'austros' (plural) are the south winds, here fair winds. 'demoror' is the present of the deponent 'demoror', 'hold back, delay', with an accusative. Helenus breaks off his own kindly talk because the fleet is waiting (the same wind as 472–473). The closing mark ” ends his speech.

sentences.t:
Nec minus Andromache digressu maesta supremo
fert picturatas auri subtemine vestes
et Phrygiam Ascanio chlamydem (nec cedit honore),
textilibusque onerat donis, ac talia fatur:
sentences.l:
Nor less Andromache at the departure sad, the last,
brings embroidered with gold thread garments
and a Phrygian for Ascanius cloak (nor does she yield in honour),
and with woven gifts loads him, and such things speaks:
sentences.i: Andromache, no less, sad at this last parting, brings garments embroidered with threads of gold, and a Phrygian cloak for Ascanius (she is not behind in honour), and loads him with woven gifts, and speaks to him thus:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Nec minus' is a litotes (a double negative that means 'equally, in her turn'): Andromache does as much as Helenus. 'digressu… supremo' is an ablative of cause, 'at the last departure'; 'maesta' ('sad') is nominative. 'picturatas auri subtemine vestes' — 'picturatas' is an accusative plural participle-adjective, 'embroidered, worked as a picture', agreeing with 'vestes'; 'subtemine' is an ablative of means, 'with a weft (thread) of gold'. 'Phrygiam Ascanio chlamydem' — 'Ascanio' is a dative of the person for whom, set between 'Phrygiam' and 'chlamydem' (accusative of 'chlamys', a Greek word for a cloak). 'nec cedit honore' — in the parenthesis, 'cedo' with an ablative of respect means 'to be inferior in': she does not give way to Helenus in the honour she shows. 'textilibusque onerat donis' — 'onerat' is 'loads', with Ascanius understood, and 'donis' an ablative of means. 'ac talia fatur' — 'fatur' is the historic present of the deponent 'for' (as in 309). The colon opens her speech to the boy.

sentences.t:
“Accipe et haec, manuum tibi quae monumenta mearum
sint, puer, et longum Andromachae testentur amorem,
coniugis Hectoreae.
sentences.l:
“Take also these, of hands (my own) to you which memorials
may be, boy, and the long love of Andromache may attest,
of the Hectorean wife.
sentences.i: “Take these too, my boy, as keepsakes of my own hands, to bear witness to the long love of Andromache, Hector's wife.
sentences.n: 'Accipe et haec' — 'haec' is neuter plural, 'these things'. 'quae… sint… et… testentur' — the relative clause has subjunctives because it states a purpose ('which are to be…'): 'sint', 'testentur'. 'monumenta' (Greenough's form; the Latin Library prints 'monimenta') is 'reminders, keepsakes', and is the predicate. 'manuum mearum' — 'manuum' is the genitive plural of 'manus'; her own hands made the gifts. 'tibi' is a dative of the person who has them; 'puer' is the vocative, to Ascanius. 'longum Andromachae testentur amorem' — 'testor' takes an accusative, 'to bear witness to'; 'longum' means 'lasting'. Andromache names herself in the third person, a formal, ceremonial manner; 'coniugis Hectoreae' is in apposition to 'Andromachae' (a genitive), 'wife of Hector' (the adjective 'Hectoreae' is made from Hector's name), the title she still gives herself.

sentences.t:
Cape dona extrema tuorum,
O mihi sola mei super Astyanactis imago:
sentences.l:
Take the gifts last of your own people,
O to me only of my Astyanax remaining likeness:
sentences.i: Take these last gifts from your kin, you who are all that is left me of my Astyanax's likeness:
sentences.n: 'Cape' is the imperative. 'dona extrema tuorum' — 'tuorum' is the genitive plural masculine of the possessive 'tuus', 'of your own people', used as a noun; 'extrema' ('last') means the final gifts she will give. 'O mihi sola mei super Astyanactis imago' — 'imago' (nominative or vocative, 'likeness') is the predicate and Ascanius the person addressed; 'mihi' is a dative, 'to me'; 'sola' agrees with 'imago'; 'super' here means 'remaining, left over', the verb 'est' being left out; 'Astyanactis' is a Greek genitive, 'of Astyanax', Hector's and Andromache's little son, who in the tradition was thrown from the walls of Troy. The colon introduces her description of how alike he was.

sentences.t: sic oculos, sic ille manus, sic ora ferebat;
sentences.l: thus his eyes, thus he his hands, thus his face bore;
sentences.i: such were his eyes, such his hands, such the look of his face;
sentences.n: 'sic… sic… sic' repeats 'thus' three times (anaphora, a kind of repetition that builds feeling); 'ille' is Astyanax, put in the middle of the series. 'ferebat' is an imperfect, 'used to carry, bear', with three objects, 'oculos', 'manus' and 'ora', governed by the one verb at the end; the sense is that he held his eyes, hands and face in this way, as Ascanius does now.

sentences.t: et nunc aequali tecum pubesceret aevo.”
sentences.l: and now of equal with you age he would be growing up.”
sentences.i: and he would be growing up now, of an age with you.”
sentences.n: 'et nunc… pubesceret' — 'pubesceret' is an imperfect subjunctive of 'pubesco', 'grow up, reach manhood', here a present contrary-to-fact statement with the condition left out ('if he were alive'). 'aequali tecum… aevo' is an ablative of description, 'of equal age with you', with 'tecum' set in the middle. The closing mark ” ends Andromache's speech, in Greenough's print placed after the full stop.

sentences.t: Hos ego digrediens lacrimis adfabar obortis:
sentences.l: These I, departing, with tears risen was addressing:
sentences.i: As I left them I spoke to them, with tears welling up:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Aeneas the narrator resumes. 'Hos' is the object, 'these' (Helenus and Andromache and their people). 'digrediens' is a present participle, 'departing'. 'adfabar' is the imperfect of the deponent 'adfor' (spelt 'adfabar'), 'I was addressing'. 'lacrimis obortis' is an ablative absolute, 'tears having arisen', from the deponent 'orior' with a prefix, 'well up'. The colon opens his reply.

sentences.t:
“Vivite felices, quibus est fortuna peracta
iam sua;
sentences.l:
“Live happy, to whom is their fortune accomplished
already their own;
sentences.i: “Live on in happiness, you whose own fortune has already run its course;
sentences.n: 'Vivite felices' — 'vivite' is the imperative; 'felices' is a predicate, 'as happy ones'. 'quibus est fortuna peracta iam sua' — 'quibus' is the dative of the people concerned, with 'est peracta' ('has been completed') a perfect passive, 'for whom their own fortune is fully run'; 'sua' ('their own') emphasises that each has their own lot. In his farewell, Aeneas contrasts them with himself ('nos', next unit).

sentences.t: nos alia ex aliis in fata vocamur.
sentences.l: we, others after others, to fates are called.
sentences.i: we are summoned onward to fate after fate.
sentences.n: 'nos' is emphatic, set against 'vobis' in the next verse. 'alia ex aliis' (one after another) puts the same word in different cases (polyptoton), 'others out of others'; 'in fata' is 'into fates'. 'vocamur' is a present passive, 'we are summoned', the language of a call or destiny. The 'fata' are the fates already laid out by Helenus, a series that will not end until Italy.

sentences.t: Vobis parta quies;
sentences.l: To you won rest;
sentences.i: Rest has been won for you;
sentences.n: 'Vobis' is a dative of the person for whom. 'parta' is a perfect passive participle of 'pario', 'gained, won', and 'est' is understood: a nominal sentence. The semicolon is followed by the things they are free of.

sentences.t:
nullum maris aequor arandum,
arva neque Ausoniae semper cedentia retro
quaerenda.
sentences.l:
no of the sea plain to be ploughed,
fields nor of Ausonia ever receding backward
to be sought.
sentences.i: no expanse of sea is left for you to furrow, and no Ausonian fields, ever slipping backward, for you to hunt.
sentences.n: 'nullum maris aequor arandum' — 'arandum' is a gerundive, 'to be ploughed', with 'est' understood, 'there is no sea-plain to be ploughed'; sailing is spoken of as ploughing, as 'aequor' means a flat surface. 'arva neque Ausoniae semper cedentia retro quaerenda' — 'quaerenda' is also a gerundive, 'to be sought', and the whole expresses what is necessary; 'vobis' ('for you') is the person who has to do it, taken over from the line before. 'arva… quaerenda' stand in different lines, framing 'Ausoniae semper cedentia retro' ('Ausonia's, always receding behind'), where 'cedentia' is a present participle (neuter plural) agreeing with 'arva' and 'retro' is an adverb, 'backward'. Italy always seems to withdraw as the Trojans approach.

sentences.t:
Effigiem Xanthi Troiamque videtis
quam vestrae fecere manus, melioribus, opto,
auspiciis, et quae fuerit minus obvia Graiis.
sentences.l:
An image of Xanthus and Troy you see, which your hands made,
under better, I pray,
auspices, and which may be less in the way of the Greeks.
sentences.i: You see a likeness of Xanthus, and a Troy that your own hands have made, under better omens, I pray, and one that may lie less open to the Greeks.
sentences.n: 'Effigiem Xanthi Troiamque videtis' — 'effigiem' is 'likeness'; Xanthus is the little stream in Buthrotum named for the river of Troy (see 350). 'Troiamque' is the object, and 'quam' is its relative. 'fecere' is 'fecerunt' (the ending -ere, you'll see this constantly). 'melioribus, opto, auspiciis' — 'melioribus… auspiciis' is an ablative of attendant circumstance, 'under better auspices' (omens), with 'opto' ('I pray') set in the middle; the new Troy was made under better auspices than the old one. 'et quae fuerit minus obvia Graiis' — 'quae' is another relative, and 'fuerit' a perfect subjunctive that carries on the wish, 'and which may be…'; 'obvia' ('in the way of, exposed to') takes the dative 'Graiis', a poetic word for 'Greeks'.

sentences.t:
Si quando Thybrim vicinaque Thybridis arva
intraro, gentique meae data moenia cernam,
cognatas urbes olim populosque propinquos,
sentences.l:
If ever Tiber and the neighbouring of Tiber fields
I shall have entered, and to my people given walls shall see,
kindred cities some day and peoples near,
sentences.i: If ever I enter the Tiber and the fields that lie near the Tiber, and see the walls granted to my people, the kindred cities, some day, and neighbouring peoples,
sentences.n: 'Si quando… intraro… cernam' — 'intraro' is a contracted future perfect ('intravero'), 'if ever I shall have entered'; 'cernam' is a future, 'I shall see'. 'Thybrim' is a Greek accusative of 'Thybris', the Tiber, and 'Thybridis' its genitive. 'gentique meae data moenia' — 'data' is a perfect passive participle (neuter plural), 'given', and 'gentique meae' a dative, 'to my people': the city promised by fate. 'cognatas urbes olim populosque propinquos' — a phrase that continues into the next lines: 'cognatas' ('related, kindred') agrees with 'urbes', and the cities and peoples are those of the two places that follow. 'olim' means 'some day'. The comma is where the sentence is cut into two.

sentences.i: in Epirus and in Hesperia, with the same Dardanus as founder and the same fortune, we shall make each Troy one, in spirit;
sentences.n: 'Epiro, Hesperia' are ablatives of place with no preposition, 'in Epirus, in Hesperia' (the Latin Library prints 'Hesperiam', which would be an accusative and would not match 'Epiro'). 'quibus idem Dardanus auctor atque idem casus' — 'quibus' is a dative of possession, 'to whom (there is) the same founder', with 'est' understood: 'idem… atque idem' ('the same… and the same') says the Trojans and the Italians share an ancestor and a lot. Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojans, came from Italy, the Penates told Aeneas (3.163–168). 'unam faciemus utramque Troiam animis' — 'unam' is a predicate, 'one', and 'utramque Troiam' ('each Troy, both Troys') is the object: 'we shall make both Troys one'. 'animis' is an ablative of respect, 'in spirit'. The two Troys are the one in Epirus, a copy, and the one that Aeneas will found.

sentences.t: maneat nostros ea cura nepotes.”
sentences.l: may await our descendants that concern.”
sentences.i: and may that concern await our descendants.”
sentences.n: 'maneat' is a present subjunctive of wish, 'may it await'; 'maneo' takes an accusative when it means 'wait for': 'nostros… nepotes' ('our descendants') is the object, and 'ea cura' ('that concern') the subject. The 'cura' is the task of joining the two Troys. 'nepotes' ('descendants') is wider than 'grandsons'. The closing mark ” ends Aeneas's speech; he is still speaking to Dido, and the next part picks up the voyage.
